STYLE: HAND-DRAWN INK AND WASH (for informal, thinking-aloud lessons; reflection; a sketchbook voice)
- A skilled illustrator's location sketch: perspective drawn by eye but sound, line drives the drawing, with real variation in weight and a slight natural wobble (no ruler-perfect lines, no shaky jitter either).
- Ink in lm-outline: the near objects in a 3 to 4 px line, the far wall in 1.5 px; lines overshoot slightly at corners; some edges are left open where the light hits.
- Wash in two or three transparent tones per material, laid loosely and not filling to the line everywhere; the paper (wall or paper colour) is left untouched where the light is strongest.
- Hatching or a darker wash only in the shadow side and under things.
- Work outside-in: the big silhouettes and the few large dark shapes first, detail last; one decisive line, not five; heavier lines on near objects, overlaps and the undersides of forms; the wash never repeats what the ink already says.
- Light: Light is the paper left white; shadow is a cool wash in the shadow colour at 0.2 to 0.3 opacity, with hatching in the deepest places.
- Texture: Paper fibres as sparse fine vector strokes in lm-texture; wash edges a little irregular (blooms) on 2 or 3 large areas.
- Depth: Far: thin line, almost no wash. Mid: line and wash. Near: the strongest line and the darkest wash.
- Quality bar: A page from a professional illustrator's sketchbook of a real office: loose, confident, specific.

THE WORLD: HISTORY AND PERIOD WORLDS
One cotton-weaving town in a temperate valley, seen at two dates in the life of its main firm. The 1890s: the firm's north-light weaving shed of about 800 looms, its counting house in the stone office block beside the shed, and the town's market street on a market day. The 1950s: the same firm's general office, in the same stone block, sixty years on. Two dates are kept on purpose and no others: the 1890s carry the origins of factory safety law, wages and records, and fair trading; the 1950s carry how office work used to be done. Every scene says which date it is.
Architecture:
- the town is built of local buff-grey sandstone, blackened by coal smoke, with blue-grey slate roofs; terraced streets climb the valley side; the firm's tall square chimney stands over the shed
- the weaving shed: one storey under a sawtooth north-light roof (glazed slopes facing north, slated slopes facing south, about 30 degrees), on a grid of slim hollow cast-iron columns carrying cast-iron gutter beams at about 3.5 m, the ridges at about 4.6 m; stone-flag floors; lime-washed stone walls; line shafts on brackets along the column rows driving cross-shafts and leather belts down to every loom
- the office block beside the shed: two storeys of dressed sandstone, tall timber sash windows with small panes, plastered walls, timber floors, panelled timber doors and partitions with glazed upper panels, a cast-iron fireplace in the principal rooms
- the market street: three-storey stone buildings with shops below, timber shop fronts with small-paned windows and painted fascia boards (slots), a wide street of stone setts with stone flag pavements and kerbs, gas street lamps on cast-iron columns, a stone drinking trough
- 1890s lighting is gas: wall brackets and pendants with glass globes; 1950s lighting is electric: opal glass pendant globes and a few fluorescent tubes
Materials: buff-grey sandstone (blackened outside, clean inside), blue-grey slate, lime-wash, cast iron painted dark green or black, oak and pitch pine joinery, brass fittings, leather (belts, ledger bindings, stool seats), cotton cloth in grey and cream, canvas awnings; in the 1950s also brown linoleum, green-grey painted steel, cream paint and Bakelite. The firm's colour is a deep bottle green (the shed's cast iron, the office doors, later the filing cabinets), with signal red only where it is red in life (a fire bucket, a pillar box on the street)

- the shed's bays about 3.6 m by 6 m between columns; 3.5 m to the gutter beams and 4.6 m to the ridges; looms about 2.1 m long, 1.0 m deep and 1.2 m high, set back to back in pairs with alleys about 0.8 m wide between their fronts; four looms to a weaver
- the office block's rooms about 3.6 m high with sash windows from a sill at 0.9 m to a head at about 2.9 m; doors about 2.1 by 0.9 m

Signs of life (every set shows someone works here):
- 1890s work in progress: cloth growing on the looms, full and empty pirns in skips, weft baskets, a weaver's shawl on a peg, ledgers open on the desks, wage packets laid out in rows (slots), produce heaped on the stalls
- 1950s work in progress: sheets wound into typewriters with carbon paper between them, files in wire trays, a teacup and saucer, an ashtray with a stubbed cigarette, a cardigan over a chair back
- the firm's systems: notices pinned at the shed door (slots), a time clock or a pay window, a fire bucket on a hook, a speaking tube in the 1890s office, a switchboard-fed telephone in the 1950s one
- wear and age: worn flags in the alleys, cotton fluff on every ledge in the shed, ink stains on desks, scuffed linoleum, a cracked pane
Default light: Daylight on an ordinary working day in autumn: in the 1890s scenes a grey, smoky, slightly golden light, soft and diffuse; in the 1950s scene a cleaner bright overcast daylight. Gas or electric lights are lit only where the scene says so.
Outside: Beyond the town: the valley sides of rough pasture with dry-stone walls, more mill chimneys down the valley with a soft haze of smoke, a pale sky.
